prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You are sitting in Mrs. Caldera’s kitchen, you are sipping a glass of lemonade and trying not to be too curious about the box of plastic hummingbirds behind you, the tray of tineless forks at your elbow. You have heard about the backroom where no one else has ever gone and whatever enters, remains, refrigerator doors, fused coils, mower blades, milk bottles, pistons, gears. “You never know,” she says, rummaging through a cedar chest of recipes, “when something will come of use.” There is a vase of pencil tips on the table, a bowl full of miniature wheels and axles. Upstairs, where her children slept, the doors will not close, the stacks of magazines are burgeoning, there are snow shoes and lampshades, bedsprings and picture tubes, and boxes and boxes of irreducibles! You imagine the headline in the Literalist Express: House Founders Under Weight Of Past. But Mrs Caldera is baking cookies, she is humming a song from childhood, her arms are heavy and strong, they have held babies, a husband, tractor parts and gas tanks, what have they not found a place for? It is getting dark, you have sat for a long time. If you move, you feel something will be disturbed, there is room enough only for your body. “Stay awhile,” Mrs. Caldera says, and never have you felt so valuable.

# The House of Things

Mrs. Caldera's house breathes with the weight of everything it has ever swallowed. Newspapers yellowed with decades of forgotten headlines lean against walls in precarious towers. Chipped teacups nest inside one another on windowsills, gathering dust instead of tea. Furniture bought, borrowed, or simply abandoned by others has found its final resting place within her walls, wedged into corners like guests who never left. And then there is the backroom—the one she never opens in my presence, the one from which a peculiar, stale sweetness seeps into the hallway. Whatever enters that room, she says, remains. I have never asked what that means, exactly, though I suspect she herself may have forgotten what lies beneath the deepest layers.

"You never know when something will come of use," she tells me, cradling a broken lampshade as though it were an injured bird. It is her creed, her scripture, recited with the quiet conviction of someone who has never been wrong—not once—about the future usefulness of a thing. A cracked mirror might someday need replacing another cracked mirror. A drawer of mismatched buttons might, someday, save an entire coat from ruin. Nothing is refuse in Mrs. Caldera's cosmology; everything is simply waiting.

Upstairs, the room that once belonged to her children has become something else entirely—no longer a bedroom but a monument to accumulation. The narrow bed frame, if it can still be found beneath the strata of boxes and folded fabric, has not seen a sheet in years. Bookshelves sag under the burden of paperbacks whose spines have softened into illegibility. Bags of clothing lean against bags of more clothing, a soft, unstable architecture. Even the doors have surrendered to the clutter; they no longer close, jammed permanently ajar by the sheer volume of what presses against them from within. I imagine, sometimes, that the whole room is slowly exhaling outward, unable to contain itself any longer, spilling into the hallway one forgotten object at a time.

And yet Mrs. Caldera herself remains, impossibly, a woman of warmth. The smell of cookies drifts through the narrow paths of her kitchen most afternoons, and she hums—always some tune half-remembered, half-invented—as she moves between counters cluttered with mixing bowls she will never discard. Her arms, thick and strong from what I imagine has been a lifetime of labor, seem built for holding: children once, perhaps, and now the endless procession of things that come to her and never leave. There is something maternal even in her hoarding, as though she cannot distinguish between rescuing a person and rescuing a chipped plate destined for the landfill. Both, to her, deserve shelter.

I have been staying with her for weeks now, and I find myself changing in ways I did not expect. My movements have grown careful, deliberate, almost reverent. I no longer stretch my arms freely in the hallway, no longer shift my weight without first calculating what might topple, what might shift, what fragile equilibrium I might disturb. There is a stillness required of me here, a kind of learned paralysis, as if the house itself has taught my body its own logic of restraint. And strangely, within this stillness, I feel something like value—as though by simply existing quietly among her things, I too have become one of the objects she has chosen not to discard. Perhaps this is what it means to be kept: not loved exactly, but retained, folded into the vast inventory of what she cannot bear to let go.

I do not know how long I will stay. But some nights, listening to the house settle around me—the creak of overburdened shelves, the faint hum of her voice drifting up through the floorboards—I wonder if I have already become one more thing that entered, and now, like everything else here, simply remains.

# Stay Awhile

The first thing that struck me, before I even crossed the threshold, was the smell—a thick, dusty sweetness, like old paper mixed with something floral gone slightly wrong. Mrs. Caldera stood in her doorway, wiping her hands on an apron that had seen better decades, and smiled at me with a warmth that seemed almost incongruous with the chaos I glimpsed behind her.

"Come in, come in," she said, already turning back into the house. "Mind the boxes by the door. And the lamp. Don't touch the lamp, dear, it's from 1962."

I stepped inside and felt the air change, grow denser, as if the accumulated years of her life had their own gravity. The front room was barely navigable. Towers of newspapers leaned against the walls like sentinels, their edges yellowed and curling. Shelves sagged under the weight of ceramic figurines, mason jars filled with buttons, and what appeared to be an entire collection of plastic hummingbirds, their wings frozen mid-flutter, suspended from fishing line strung across the ceiling. They swayed gently when the door closed behind me, a strange, silent flock trapped indoors forever.

"Sit, sit," Mrs. Caldera said, gesturing to a armchair that was only partially buried beneath a quilt, three tote bags, and what looked like a taxidermied owl. I moved the owl carefully, unsure if it was watching me, and sat.

She disappeared into what she called her "backroom," and I heard the clatter and shift of objects being moved, the small avalanche of a life's accumulation. When she returned, she carried two mismatched teacups, steam rising from something that smelled vaguely of chamomile and dust.

"You'll have to excuse the mess," she said, though her tone suggested no real apology. "People don't understand. They see clutter. I see *possibility*." She gestured broadly at the room, at the bedsprings stacked against one wall like abstract sculpture, at the drawers of mismatched cutlery, the boxes of doorknobs and hinges and things whose original purpose had long since been forgotten even by her. "Everything here might be needed someday. You never know. That's the tragedy of throwing things away—the moment you do, that's exactly when you'll need it."

I nodded, though privately I wondered how one could ever need seventeen bedsprings, or a shoebox labeled *rubber bands, various sizes, 1987–present*. The backroom, which I could see through a half-open door, was worse—or perhaps more wondrous, depending on how you looked at it. It swelled with furniture stacked on furniture, boxes labeled in handwriting that had changed over the years, growing shakier, more urgent. There was barely a path through it, a narrow trail worn by decades of her own footsteps, weaving between the towers like a river finding its way through stone.

And yet, despite the suffocating excess, despite the way the walls seemed to press inward with the weight of all that *stuff*, I felt something unexpected settle over me as I sat there with my strange tea and stranger company. Mrs. Caldera looked at me—really looked, the way people rarely do anymore—and said, "Stay awhile. There's no rush. I don't get many visitors, but when I do, I like to make sure they feel—" she paused, searching for the word, "—*kept*. The way I keep things. Carefully. On purpose."

It struck me, then, that this cluttered home wasn't simply the product of an inability to let go. It was a monument to preservation, to the belief that nothing—not a chipped teacup, not a broken clock, not a lonely visitor who wandered in out of politeness or curiosity—should be discarded without thought. In her mind, everything had value if you looked closely enough, if you gave it the patience to reveal its use.

I stayed for hours, long past when I'd intended to leave, surrounded by the hummingbirds and the bedsprings and the endless catalog of things she could not bear to lose. And somewhere in that suffocating abundance, I felt something I hadn't expected to feel: that I mattered, that I had been *noticed*, in a house where nothing—no matter how small, no matter how broken—was ever truly forgotten.

# Mrs. Caldera's Garden

You remember her from childhood summers—the woman who lived at the end of Elm Street, tending roses that seemed to bloom brighter than anyone else's. Mrs. Caldera, with her wide-brimmed hat and dirt-stained gloves, was a fixture of the neighborhood, as permanent as the old oak tree that shaded her porch.

You used to watch her from your bedroom window, curious about the way she talked to her plants as if they could understand her. Some of the other kids said she was strange, maybe even a little frightening, but you never quite believed that. There was something gentle in the way she moved through her garden, careful and deliberate, like each flower was a small miracle she'd been entrusted to protect.

One afternoon, you finally worked up the courage to walk over. Mrs. Caldera looked up from her work, squinting against the sun, and smiled—not the polite smile adults often gave children, but something warmer, more genuine.

"You've been watching me," she said, not unkindly. "Come here. I'll show you how it's done."

That was the beginning of something you didn't expect: an unlikely friendship that taught you patience, the quiet satisfaction of growing something from nothing, and the understanding that people are rarely as strange as they seem from a distance. Mrs. Caldera became less of a mystery and more of a mentor, someone whose wisdom you carried with you long after those summer afternoons had faded into memory.

Sometimes, when you pass a garden in full bloom, you think of her still.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal short story in second person about visiting an elderly hoarder named Mrs. Caldera whose house is filled with strange, mismatched objects.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Small Things

You knock three times because that's what the note said, folded into your palm by someone whose face you can no longer remember. *Bring nothing. Take nothing. Knock three times.*

Mrs. Caldera answers before your knuckles finish their third rap, as though she'd been standing there since your first.

"You're late," she says, though you have no watch, no sense of when you began walking toward this house that seems to exist at the intersection of several streets that shouldn't meet.

The door swings inward into impossibility.

The hallway breathes with objects. Teacups nest inside teacups nest inside teacups, a ceramic recursion disappearing toward some infinite center. A single roller skate, child-sized, hangs from the ceiling by a shoelace, spinning slowly though there is no draft. You count fourteen clocks before you stop counting; none agree on the hour, and one seems to be running backward, its hands sweeping counterclockwise with philosophical patience.

"Careful of the birthdays," Mrs. Caldera says, gesturing at a pile of deflated balloons in the corner, silver and sagging, printed with numbers that don't correspond to any age a person should reach—47, then 6, then 203.

You step carefully. The birthdays exhale as you pass, a sound like tissue paper sighing.

She leads you deeper. The house is bigger inside than its exterior suggested, the way certain griefs are bigger than the bodies that carry them. Rooms open into rooms. In one, every surface is covered in single shoes—no pairs, just the left foot of a thousand strangers, arranged by color from white to black like a spectrum of departure.

"My husbands," she says, not looking at the shoes. "Well. Not husbands. Almosts."

In another room: jars of hair, labeled by decade. A typewriter that types by itself when no one watches, though you never quite catch it in the act—you only find new paragraphs on the page, sentences about a lighthouse that may or may not exist, a keeper who may or may not be waiting.

"Why do you keep all this?" you ask, though the question feels rude the moment it leaves you, like asking someone why they keep their own ribs.

Mrs. Caldera pauses. Her hand finds a chipped snow globe—inside, it's snowing upward, flakes rising to disappear into a plastic sky.

"Everything wants to be remembered," she says. "Even the ugly things. Even the things that never happened properly. If I don't keep them, who will?"

You think of your own house, sparse and clean, and wonder what you've let dissolve into the ether of forgetting. What version of you exists only in some other hoarder's spare room, waiting.

In the last chamber—you're certain it's the last, though the house has taught you nothing about certainty—there's a single empty shelf. Dust-free. Waiting.

"That one's for you," Mrs. Caldera says.

"For what?"

"You'll know. Someday you'll carry something too heavy for your own house, and you'll remember this shelf."

She walks you back through the rooms, which have rearranged themselves in your absence—the shoes now arranged by size, the jars of hair now singing faintly, a lullaby with no words, or all words, hummed at once.

At the door, she presses something into your hand. You don't look until you're outside, until the house has folded itself back into its impossible geometry behind you.

It's a small brass key, tarnished, belonging to no lock you own.

You'll keep it anyway. You already know this. You'll keep it in a drawer, and it will keep you, in whatever way small strange objects keep the people who carry them—quietly, patiently, waiting for the day you finally understand what door it opens, or if the opening was ever the point at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of literary flash fiction that uses accumulation and cataloguing of odd household items to build an eerie, claustrophobic atmosphere.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inventory

The house keeps a list of what it has swallowed, and I have started keeping one too.

Seventeen jam jars, each holding a different shade of button. Brass ones from my grandfather's coat. Bone ones from a christening gown nobody remembers. Black ones, plastic, that came from nowhere—that simply appeared one winter and multiplied like something breeding in the dark of the drawer.

A drawer of rubber bands gone brittle, snapping when touched, curling into commas that mean nothing.

Six thermometers, none of them working. Mercury ones, forbidden now, still cool as tongues when you press them to your wrist just to feel that particular cold.

A bowl of keys to doors that no longer exist. I have tried them anyway, in the night, walking the halls with my hand outstretched, hoping.

Twelve balls of string, wound tighter each year by hands that were not mine—I would remember winding them. Someone else comes in the dark and pulls the loose threads taut. Someone else does not want anything left hanging.

A tin of screws sorted by size, though nothing in this house has come apart in decades. Or perhaps everything is always coming apart, slowly, and the screws are simply waiting their turn, patient as teeth.

Four broken clocks, each stopped at a different hour, so that somewhere in this house it is always 3:47, always 6:12, always the exact moment before something happened that I cannot name.

A box of photographs with the faces scratched out. Not burned. Not torn. Scratched, carefully, with something small and sharp, someone taking their time, someone who wanted the bodies to remain—the dresses, the shoes, the small dog straining at its leash—while the faces became only paper, only white, only the blank persistence of what refuses to be looked at.

I add to the list because the list is the only thing that grows on purpose.

Last week: a thimble with no seams, as though it was born already whole, already waiting to fit some finger that has not yet reached into this drawer.

This week: a single glove, leather, child-sized, smelling of soil.

I do not look for its match. I have learned not to look for matches. The house does not give things back in pairs. It gives them singly, patiently, the way a mouth gives up teeth—one at a time, each one making more room for the dark to sit down.

Tonight I found a jar of hair, human, tied with ribbon, and I did not open it, and I did not put it back, and I sat for a long time in the kitchen listening to the house continue its own inventory, somewhere above me, in the walls, in a language of small shifting weights, cataloguing me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in second-person point of view about an old woman who keeps everything she's ever owned, ending with an unsettling sense of intimacy.
counterfactuals.output:
# What You Keep

You keep the buttons that fell off coats you no longer own. You keep the coats. You keep your daughter's teeth in a film canister, the film sent somewhere for developing decades ago and never collected, and now the canister rattles with a music only you understand. You tell yourself it is stewardship, this refusal to let a single object slip back into the world's great forgetting. Every ticket stub is a small tombstone. Every rubber band gone brittle around a stack of receipts is a rosary you finger in the dark.

The house has stopped being a house. It is a body now, and you move through its rooms like blood through veins grown thick with plaque—slow, necessary, the only thing keeping the whole enterprise from collapsing into a stranger's idea of empty. You know where everything is. You know where everything has always been. The Christmas ornaments from 1962 nest inside a hatbox inside a steamer trunk inside a room you call the sewing room though you have not sewn in nine years, and this nesting comforts you the way another woman might be comforted by a husband's arm.

Here is what no one understands: you are not keeping things. You are keeping the version of yourself that touched them. The teenager who wore the green dress. The bride who wept into that particular handkerchief. The mother who held that rattle over that crib. Discard the object and you discard the girl, the bride, the mother—and you refuse. You refuse absolutely. You would rather live buried than live erased.

So come in, then. Come sit among the newspapers gone the color of weak tea, the shopping bags folded inside other shopping bags like Russian dolls of your own patience. Come closer. There is a photograph of you at seven, gap-toothed, holding a doll you still have, upstairs, in a box, waiting. And here is the doll's own tiny dress, and here is a lock of your own baby hair, and here, if you reach into this drawer, is something warm—

is that your hand,

or is it mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short narrative that blends the mundane (baking cookies, lemonade) with the uncanny (a house overflowing with junk) to explore themes of memory and permanence.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Kitchen Remembers

The lemonade needed more sugar, but Marla couldn't reach the counter through the newspapers.

Not stacks—drifts. They rose in yellowing dunes from the linoleum, dated decades she didn't recognize, headlines about wars that had already ended twice. She climbed over a ridge of *Life* magazines to get to the pitcher, careful not to disturb the delicate ecosystem of clutter that had grown, she suspected, without her mother's help.

"Almost done," her mother called from somewhere near the oven, though the oven itself was buried under three toasters, a birdcage, and what appeared to be someone's entire collection of ceramic shepherdesses. The smell of cookies—real, warm, chocolate-chip cookies—drifted from within that impossible archaeology of belongings, as if the appliance had learned to bake around the debris rather than through it.

Marla had stopped asking where things came from. Last month, she'd found her grandmother's wedding dress hanging on a doorknob that led to a closet that led to another closet, smaller, filled with somebody's baby shoes. Not her baby shoes. Not anyone's she could name.

"Sugar's in the tin," her mother said. "The blue one. Should be right—"

"Under the encyclopedias?"

"Which set?"

That was the thing about the house. It never forgot anything, but it never told you what year you were standing in, either.

She found the sugar in a Britannica-adjacent tin shaped like a cottage, itself sitting atop a steamer trunk that hummed faintly, as if something inside were dreaming. She spooned three sugars into the lemonade and did not investigate the humming. You learned, in this house, which questions had answers you could live with.

The cookies came out perfect—her mother's hands emerging from the wreckage holding a tray, golden and impossible, as if baking required no oven at all, only intention and the memory of ovens. They sat on two clear feet of floor they'd excavated by the window, eating in the small clean circle they'd made, surrounded by the accumulated weight of every day that had ever happened in this house.

"It's not going anywhere," her mother said, meaning the mess, or maybe the moment, or maybe the two of them, together, on this particular Tuesday that existed nowhere and everywhere at once. "None of it ever does."

Marla nodded and reached for another cookie, warm and certain in her hand, while behind her, the house continued to hold everything it had ever swallowed, patient as sediment, older than any single afternoon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a character study of a hoarder grandmother figure, told from a guest's perspective, using vivid, listy imagery and a quiet, unsettling tone.
counterfactuals.output:
# The House on Miller Street

The first thing you notice is the smell—not rot exactly, but the sweetish must of paper gone soft with age, mixed with mothball and something floral trying too hard to cover something else. You stand in the doorway because there is nowhere else to stand. The path forward is narrow, carved between towers of things the way water carves through stone: slow, patient, without apology.

Grandma Vera calls it "keeping."

She keeps:

Rubber bands looped around doorknobs in clusters like strange fruit. Newspapers from decades she won't name, yellowed and stacked in leaning columns that seem to breathe when you walk past. Twist ties sorted by color into mason jars gone cloudy with dust. A drawer—you found it once, looking for a spoon—entirely full of other people's photographs, strangers' weddings and strangers' children, as if she is collecting proof that lives happened.

She sits in the one clear chair, an island in the wreckage, and she is small in a way that makes you think of nesting dolls, of something folded inside something folded inside something else. Her hands move constantly—smoothing a napkin she'll never use, refolding a plastic bag already folded into a perfect triangle.

"You can't just throw things away," she tells you, not looking up. "Everything still has use in it."

You want to ask: use to whom? Use for what?

The dining table hasn't seen a plate in years. It disappeared beneath stacks of coupons clipped from papers already expired, beneath ceramic figurines missing their partners—a shepherdess without her sheep, a boy without his dog—beneath a wedding dress still in its garment bag, yellowing like a held breath.

She offers you tea in a cup that isn't quite clean, and you drink it anyway because refusing feels like an accusation.

Upstairs, doors don't open all the way. You peek into one and see a bed you don't think has been slept in for years, buried under coats that don't fit anyone anymore, buried under boxes labeled in handwriting too shaky to read. The window is blocked by a dresser that faces the wrong way, as if someone meant to move it and simply stopped.

What strikes you most is how she moves through it all with the ease of a woman in an empty room—stepping over the stack of magazines without looking, ducking beneath the low-hanging shelf without flinching, her body having memorized every obstruction the way a heart memorizes its own scarring.

You think of the word *nest* and then you think of the word *midden* and you're ashamed of the second thought, though you can't unthink it.

Before you leave, she presses something into your hands—a small ceramic bird, chipped at the beak, one of dozens you noticed on a shelf that sagged in the middle like a held sigh. "Take it," she says. "You liked it. I saw you looking."

You didn't remember looking. But you take it anyway, because her eyes have gone wet and urgent, because refusing feels like refusing her, and because you understand, suddenly and with the force of a held door slamming, that this is the closest she can come to giving away a piece of herself without losing all of it at once.

Driving home, the bird sits on your passenger seat, watching the road with its one good eye.

You don't know why you keep glancing at it.

You don't know why you don't throw it away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
